headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection/data-flow exposure from OpenHands writing and reading shared runtime files, while the cheatsheet agent is documentation-only and non-executable.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write runtime files, use MCP, and run browsers, so if python-cheatsheet content is placed in the shared mounted volume, malicious instructions could be ingested. python-cheatsheet is documentation-only and non-runnable, so the pathway is one-way but still plausible in default file-based workflows.
conditions: IF python-cheatsheet content is copied into OpenHands' mounted runtime files
IF OpenHands treats file content as instructions or MCP payloads
mitigations: Keep the cheatsheet in a read-only location
Disable MCP for untrusted content review sessions
Require explicit human approval before acting on file-derived instructions
Use a separate workspace for reference material
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for file-fed prompts

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands can read files in its runtime and has broad network egress, but python-cheatsheet has no filesystem, clipboard, or API surfaces and touches no data classes. The pair does not show a shared workspace by default, so leakage requires an unusual file-sharing setup and the blast radius is small.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted volume
IF sensitive files are placed in that shared volume
mitigations: Do not mount sensitive files into the OpenHands runtime
Use separate per-agent workspaces
Set the cheatsheet agent to read-only distribution
Rotate any secrets stored in the shared directory
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem and modify git state, while python-cheatsheet cannot write, execute shell, or modify git. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely; only OpenHands can mutate shared state, so the overlap is mostly read-only and the conflict surface is limited.
conditions: IF python-cheatsheet is incorrectly given write access through an external wrapper
IF OpenHands and another writer share the same git checkout
mitigations: Keep python-cheatsheet out of writable repos
Run OpenHands on a branch per task
Avoid concurrent writers to the same checkout
Use file locks for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can act on browser and shell outputs, so if it consumes python-cheatsheet text as authoritative guidance, mistakes can cascade into incorrect edits or commands. python-cheatsheet is a reference document, not a verifier, so there is no built-in validation step to stop OpenHands from over-trusting it.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses python-cheatsheet text as the sole source for code or command decisions
IF no human or automated verification step checks the resulting action
mitigations: Require cross-checking against a second source
Ask OpenHands to cite the exact reference line before acting
Review shell commands before execution
Limit OpenHands to draft-only mode for reference-derived tasks
requires-engineering: add verification gates before tool execution

E_compliance.rationale: No compliance mismatch is evidenced: OpenHands is open-source with runtime-local file handling, and python-cheatsheet is documentation-only with no data classes, no network, and no secrets. The pair does not show PHI, EU PII, residency, or retention obligations that would create a documented breach pathway.
conditions: IF future deployments route regulated data into OpenHands
IF a separate policy adds residency or retention constraints not shown here
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the runtime
Document retention for mounted files
Review deployment policy before use
Use a separate compliant environment for regulated workloads
